lessons.title: Risk management and data governance
lessons.subtitle: Risk management as an ongoing process, and the rules for training data
keyConcepts: Risk-management system as an iterative process (Article 9)
Special-category data exception for bias correction (Article 10(5))

sections.title: The risk-management system is never finished
sections.content:
**Blocks 3 to 6 are for people who buy, run or answer for AI systems at work.** If you only want the framework and your own rights, you can stop after block 2.

---

For high-risk AI systems, Article 9(1) requires a risk-management system that is **established, implemented, documented and maintained**: a continuous, iterative process across the whole lifecycle, systematically reviewed and updated (Article 9(2)). It has four steps (Article 9(2), points (a) to (d)):

- **(a)** identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights
- **(b)** estimate and evaluate risks under reasonably foreseeable misuse
- **(c)** evaluate other risks identified through post-market monitoring (Article 72)
- **(d)** adopt appropriate and targeted risk-management measures

Measures follow a ranking (Article 9(5), second subparagraph): design the risk out first, then mitigate and control, then inform and train under Article 13. Testing before market placement is mandatory (Article 9(8)), and the impact on people under 18 has to be considered (Article 9(9)).

**In practice for SMEs:** one risk matrix with the risk, likelihood, severity, control, owner and model version. Review it, for example, quarterly; the Regulation does not prescribe that interval.

Name an owner with a role and start date; that is not required, but you can show it. Infringements of the obligations in Article 99(4) can cost up to EUR 15 million or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover.

sections.title: Data governance under Article 10
sections.content:
Training, validation and testing data sets carry quality criteria (Article 10(1)); for systems built without model training, they apply only to testing data (Article 10(6)). You must document eight practices (Article 10(2), points (a) to (h)):

- (a) relevant design choices
- (b) data collection and origin; for personal data, also the original purpose
- (c) data preparation (annotation, labelling, cleaning, enrichment, aggregation)
- (d) assumptions about what the data represents
- (e) assessment of availability, quantity and suitability
- (f) examination of possible biases affecting health, safety, fundamental rights or leading to prohibited discrimination
- (g) measures to detect, prevent and mitigate them
- (h) identification and handling of data gaps

Data sets must be **relevant, sufficiently representative and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete** (Article 10(3)), and reflect the setting the system is intended for (Article 10(4)).

**In practice for SMEs:** keep one data sheet per data set along the lines of Annex IV, point 2(d), with source, acquisition method, size, principal characteristics, labelling and cleaning steps. A set from Hugging Face or Kaggle gets the same sheet as your own.

sections.title: Special-category data for bias correction and the GDPR link
sections.content:
As an exception to Article 9 GDPR, Article 10(5) allows special categories of personal data (such as ethnic origin, health or religion) to be processed to detect and correct bias where that is strictly necessary and synthetic or anonymised data will not do. All six conditions (Article 10(5), points (a) to (f)) must hold at once:

- (a) the bias cannot be detected and corrected effectively with other data
- (b) pseudonymisation and state-of-the-art security
- (c) strict access control and confidentiality obligations
- (d) no transfer to or access by other parties
- (e) deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends
- (f) an entry in the Article 30 GDPR records of processing explaining why the processing was strictly necessary

**In practice for SMEs:** to test your recruitment system for sex-related bias, you may use data about sex this way if you document the conditions and bring in the data protection officer where the GDPR requires it. Article 10(5) does not name consent as a condition, and the rest of data-protection law still applies.

Variance and subgroup analysis can detect bias, and mitigation can come before, during or after training.

quiz.questionText: Which statement about the risk-management system under Article 9 is correct?

answerOptions.text: A one-off analysis before market placement is enough if archived
A continuous, iterative process across the whole lifecycle (Article 9(2))
Only needed when the system is a safety component under Annex I
A task for the notified body, not the provider

quiz.explanation: Article 9(2) requires a continuous process across the whole lifecycle, and the provider is responsible.

quiz.questionText: Which measure does Article 10(2) NOT expressly require for training, validation, and testing data sets?

answerOptions.text: Data preparation such as annotation and cleaning (point (c))
Examining possible discriminatory biases (point (f))
A statement of the training data's carbon footprint
Identifying and addressing data gaps (point (h))

quiz.explanation: A carbon footprint is not among the eight practices in Article 10(2). Energy-consumption information belongs to the GPAI documentation in Annex XI.

quiz.questionText: When may a provider process special-category data, such as ethnic origin, to correct bias?

answerOptions.text: Whenever bias is suspected while training a high-risk system
Only when all six conditions in Article 10(5) are met at once
Only with every data subject's written consent
Only after a notified body has approved it

quiz.explanation: Article 10(5) applies only when all six conditions hold at once; it does not require consent.

lessons.title: Technical documentation and logs
lessons.subtitle: What Annex IV asks for, and why your system needs a flight recorder
keyConcepts: Annex IV as the minimum documentation structure
Retention: 10 years for provider records, at least 6 months for deployer logs

sections.title: Annex IV: what the technical documentation must contain
sections.content:
The technical documentation, your central evidence for market surveillance, is drawn up **before the system is placed on the market or put into service** and kept up to date from then on (Article 11(1)).

**SME simplification** (Article 11(1), second subparagraph): microenterprises and small and medium-sized enterprises may supply the Annex IV elements in simplified form through a Commission form that notified bodies must accept. Every required subject stays in.

**The nine main parts of Annex IV:**

- (1) general description: intended purpose, provider, version, forms of distribution
- (2) system elements and development process: methods, architecture, data requirements, human oversight, validation, cybersecurity
- (3) monitoring, functioning and control, including accuracy for relevant persons or groups
- (4) appropriateness of the performance metrics
- (5) the risk-management system under Article 9
- (6) relevant changes over the lifecycle
- (7) harmonised standards and other specifications applied
- (8) a copy of the EU declaration of conformity
- (9) the post-market monitoring plan under Article 72

Article 18(1) requires keeping it for **10 years** after market placement. Version it release by release like source code, in a repository with an audit trail.

sections.title: Automatic recording: event logs under Article 12
sections.content:
Article 12(1) makes automatic event recording a **design requirement**. Like a built-in flight recorder, the system records relevant events over its lifetime.

The logs serve to identify risk situations and substantial modifications under Article 79(1), to support post-market monitoring under Article 72 and to let the deployer monitor operation under Article 26(5) (Article 12(2)). Remote biometric identification systems under Annex III, point 1(a), must log at least (Article 12(3), points (a) to (d)):

- (a) the period of each use, with start and end date and time
- (b) the reference database the input data was checked against
- (c) the input data that produced a match
- (d) the persons who verified the results under Article 14(5)

Deployers keep the logs for at least **six months** (Article 26(6)), unless other Union or national law, including data-protection law, provides otherwise.

**In practice for SMEs:** machine-readable logs, filled automatically, exportable for market surveillance and ideally append-only, since a log that can be edited afterwards is weak evidence. Article 12 prescribes no product; Splunk, the Elastic Stack or Wazuh are options.

sections.title: Provider and deployer: who documents what
sections.content:
The **provider** prepares the Annex IV documentation before market placement, keeps logs under its control (Article 19) and keeps the EU declaration of conformity for 10 years (Article 47(1)).

The **deployer** monitors operation according to the instructions for use, keeps logs under its control for at least 6 months and reports serious incidents without undue delay to the provider and the market surveillance authority (Article 26(5) and (6)).

The Article 73 deadlines bind the provider: 15 days as standard, 2 days for a widespread infringement, 10 days in the event of a death.

**Change of role** (Article 25): whoever makes a **substantial modification** to a high-risk system or changes its intended purpose can become the provider, with Annex IV documentation and its own conformity assessment. Fine-tuning or retraining is not automatically a substantial modification; assess it against Article 3(23), the changes the original provider planned for and Article 25.

**In practice for SMEs:** run a bought recruitment tool as supplied and you are the deployer. Fine-tune it on your applicant data or change its purpose, and document the Article 25 assessment.

quiz.questionText: What must the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system contain at minimum?

answerOptions.text: A two-page summary of business model and target market
The nine main parts of Annex IV, kept current (Article 11(1))
Only the EU declaration of conformity under Annex V
Only a copy of the instructions for use under Article 13

quiz.explanation: Annex IV sets nine required parts; SMEs may supply them through the Commission's simplified form.

quiz.questionText: How long must a deployer keep a high-risk system's automatically generated logs under its control?

answerOptions.text: 24 hours after use ends
At least six months, unless other law provides otherwise (Article 26(6))
10 years after market placement, like the declaration of conformity
Until the system's next major update

quiz.explanation: Article 26(6) sets six months as the floor, and other law can differ. The 10 years apply to the provider's declaration of conformity.

quiz.questionText: A company fine-tunes a purchased AI recruitment tool on its own applicant data. What applies to its role?

answerOptions.text: It always stays a deployer; fine-tuning is legally irrelevant
It assesses under Article 25 whether the change is substantial; if so, it becomes provider
It becomes an importer under Article 23
It is responsible only for logs, never for documentation

quiz.explanation: Fine-tuning is not automatically a substantial modification; Article 3(23) and Article 25 decide whether the role changes.

lessons.title: Human oversight, accuracy, and cybersecurity
lessons.subtitle: Human control over high-risk systems and protection against attacks
keyConcepts: Two-person verification for remote biometric identification (Article 14(5))
Accuracy and robustness as design requirements (Article 15)

sections.title: Human oversight: from the concept to the stop control
sections.content:
Article 14(1) requires high-risk systems to be designed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while they are in use. Oversight is therefore a **design requirement**.

The measures come from two sources (Article 14(3)): the provider builds them in before market placement, such as interface controls, confidence information or a stop function. The deployer implements the ones the provider identifies, such as roles, training under Article 4 and escalation paths.

The overseers must be able, as appropriate and proportionate, to (Article 14(4), points (a) to (e)):

- (a) **understand** the system's capacities and limitations and detect anomalies
- (b) stay **aware of automation bias**, the tendency to rely automatically on AI output
- (c) **interpret** the output correctly
- (d) **decide not to use** the system, or disregard, override or reverse its output
- (e) **intervene or stop the system** through a stop control or comparable safe procedure

**Independent verification** (Article 14(5)): for remote biometric identification under Annex III, point 1(a), no action may rest on the AI identification alone. At least two competent, trained and authorised people must verify and confirm it separately. Law enforcement, migration, border control and asylum are exempt where Union or national law treats the rule as disproportionate.

**In practice for SMEs:** with remote biometric identification at a site entrance, a match alone opens no door.

sections.title: Accuracy and resilience: what an appropriate level means
sections.content:
Article 15(1) requires an **appropriate level** of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity across the whole lifecycle, and Article 8(1) ties that to the generally acknowledged state of the art. Harmonised standards under Article 40 create a presumption of conformity for the requirements they cover.

The provider declares accuracy levels and metrics in the instructions for use (Article 15(3)).

The system must be as resilient as possible to errors, faults and inconsistencies (Article 15(4)), for example through backup models or fail-safe paths. Where it keeps learning in operation, **feedback loops**, in which biased outputs become future inputs, need mitigation.

**In practice for SMEs:** set performance criteria before release, such as F1 >= 0.85 on a hold-out set that reflects the deployment setting; the Regulation does not set that universal threshold.

Monitor performance and drift in operation, and wire a threshold breach into the retraining or rollback plan of your post-market monitoring (Article 72). Until harmonised standards are published, document the state-of-the-art basis you chose.

sections.title: Cybersecurity: four AI-specific attack classes
sections.content:
Article 15(5) requires high-risk systems to be **resilient** against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities. The paragraph names four AI-specific threats:

- **data poisoning:** manipulating training data before or during training
- **model poisoning:** manipulating trained model components, including backdoors
- **adversarial examples or model evasion:** crafted inputs that force incorrect outputs
- **confidentiality attacks:** model inversion or membership inference to extract training information

The BSI white paper *Bias in AI* (July 2025) shows that bias can be exploited deliberately for data poisoning.

**In practice for SMEs:** run adversarial tests on a risk-based cadence and record method, scope, findings and remediation. Annual can be a sensible baseline, and Article 15 does not prescribe a universal interval. Open tools include ART from IBM and CleverHans.

For a third-party model, for example from Hugging Face, read the model card, record the hash, scan for backdoors (STRIP, Neural Cleanse) and pin the version; test again before each upstream update. The test evidence belongs in the technical documentation under Annex IV, point 2(g).

quiz.questionText: Which combination describes the five oversight capabilities in Article 14(4)?

answerOptions.text: Understand capacities, know automation bias, interpret, override output, stop
Notify provider, manager, DPO, works council and IT
Read code, debug, tune hyperparameters, retrain, roll back
Read docs, get trained, keep a log, report, escalate

quiz.explanation: Article 14(4), points (a) to (e), names exactly these five capabilities. Notification chains and technical maintenance are useful but not part of that list.

quiz.questionText: What does the separate-verification rule in Article 14(5) require?

answerOptions.text: Four people approve every AI output before use
For remote biometric identification, two authorised people separately confirm a match
Provider and deployer each appoint two overseers
Two people buy the system and two maintain it

quiz.explanation: Under Article 14(5) no action may rest on a remote biometric identification alone, with narrow exceptions such as law enforcement.

quiz.questionText: Which attack is NOT one of the four AI-specific threats identified in Article 15(5)?

answerOptions.text: Data poisoning (manipulated training data)
Model poisoning (manipulated model components)
Email phishing directed at end users
Adversarial examples or model evasion

quiz.explanation: Article 15(5) names data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples and confidentiality attacks. Phishing targets people and stays a security issue outside Article 15.

lessons.title: Conformity assessment and CE marking
lessons.subtitle: When a notified body is involved, and how CE marking reaches an API
keyConcepts: Internal control (Annex VI) and notified-body assessment (Annex VII)
EU declaration of conformity retained for 10 years (Article 47)
Registration in the EU database (Articles 49 and 71)

sections.title: Which procedure applies? The decision logic in Article 43
sections.content:
The procedure depends on the Annex III category (Article 43):

- **Annex III, point 1 (biometrics):** where the provider has applied harmonised standards (Article 40) or common specifications (Article 41), it chooses between internal control under Annex VI and a notified body under Annex VII. Article 43(1) sets out when the notified body is required.
- **Annex III, points 2 to 8:** internal control under Annex VI (Article 43(2)), with no notified body.
- **Products under Annex I, section A** (machinery, medical devices, motor vehicles, toys): the sectoral procedure absorbs the AI requirements (Article 43(3)).

Under **internal control (Annex VI)** the provider itself checks the quality-management system under Article 17, the technical documentation and its consistency with development and post-market monitoring; no third party checks first.

A **notified body (Annex VII)** assesses the quality-management system and technical documentation, carries out surveillance and may obtain access to training, validation and testing data, including through an API. Its certificate is valid for at most four years for Annex III systems (Article 44(2)).

**In practice for SMEs:** recruitment AI (point 4), credit scoring (point 5) and education (point 3) run through Annex VI. For biometrics at a site entrance (point 1(a)), check the Article 43(1) conditions closely. Find notified bodies through the accreditation authority (DAkkS in Germany) and the Commission's NANDO database.

sections.title: EU declaration of conformity and CE marking
sections.content:
**EU declaration of conformity** (Article 47):

- in writing, machine-readable, signed physically or electronically
- kept for **10 years** after market placement or putting into service (Article 47(1))
- content under Annex V: system identification, statement of conformity, standards applied, provider details
- where several Union acts apply (for example the Machinery Regulation and the AI Act), one declaration that names them all

**CE marking** (Article 48):

- visible, legible and indelible, following the principles in Article 30 of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008
- where that is impossible on the system, on the packaging or accompanying documentation
- for systems supplied digitally, a **digital** marking reached through the interface or a machine-readable code (Article 48(2))
- with the notified body's identification number where one was involved, also in promotional material (Article 48(4))

**In practice for SMEs:** for SaaS or an API, place the CE marking and a link to the declaration where users reach them, such as the login page or the licence document. On premises, put a label on the server rack and a CE notice in the software.

Incorrect or missing CE marking is formal non-compliance (Article 83); incorrect information to authorities or notified bodies can cost up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% of total worldwide annual turnover (Article 99(5)).

sections.title: Registration in the EU database under Articles 49 and 71
sections.content:
Once the high-risk rules apply, providers of Annex III systems register themselves and the system in the EU database under Article 71 **before placing it on the market or putting it into service** (Article 49(1)). Annex III, point 2 systems (critical infrastructure) are registered nationally (Article 49(5)). Public-authority deployers of Annex III systems register as well.

Annex VIII, section A, requires provider details, trade name, intended purpose, status, standards applied, a copy of the declaration of conformity and electronic instructions for use. The Commission controls the database (Article 71(6)); it is public and machine-readable, apart from non-public sections for specified public-authority uses.

A new conformity assessment may be required where an assessed system is substantially modified (Article 43(4)). After every material update, record whether a new assessment or registration is needed.

**For deployers:** applying your own CE marking is not automatically your duty. Read the provider's documentation and EU declaration of conformity, and assess any change of role under Article 25.

quiz.questionText: An SME develops an AI recruitment tool, high-risk under Annex III, point 4(a). Which procedure applies?

answerOptions.text: A notified body under Annex VII, with a four-year certificate
Internal control under Annex VI (Article 43(2))
TÜV certification, whatever the category
Only EU database registration, no procedure

quiz.explanation: For Annex III, points 2 to 8, including HR, Article 43(2) prescribes internal control.

quiz.questionText: For how long must the provider keep the EU declaration of conformity for a high-risk AI system?

answerOptions.text: Six months, like the deployer's log period (Article 26(6))
Four years, like a notified body's certificate (Article 44(2))
10 years after market placement (Article 47(1))
Until the first substantial modification

quiz.explanation: Article 47(1) requires 10 years. Six months applies to deployer logs, four years to notified-body certificates.

quiz.questionText: Where is an Annex III high-risk AI system, other than point 2, registered before market placement?

answerOptions.text: With Germany's Federal Office for Information Security (BSI)
In the Commission's EU database under Article 71, with Annex VIII data
With the German Patent and Trade Mark Office (DPMA)
With the provider's local chamber of commerce

quiz.explanation: Article 49(1) requires registration in the EU database under Article 71; only Annex III, point 2 is registered nationally.
